subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Last month I made a list, because my head was a mess. Three lies in one week.
One: my mother said she loved the sari I gave her. It is still in its bag in her cupboard.
Two: someone on my team said his train was late, again, when I'd seen him at the tea stall at ten.
Three: Ira, my flatmate, said she'd paid her half of the rent. She hadn't, for the third month running; each time the transfer was "stuck".
I sorted them. The sari was kindness; I let it go completely. The train was a small pattern, so I mentioned it once, lightly.
Ira's was different: real money, repeated, told to my face. I told her calmly that from next month the rent comes to me by the first, or I start looking for a new flatmate.
She cried. I felt terrible. I didn't change it.
Yash

qa.q: How many months running had Ira not paid her half of the rent?
qa.a: Ira had not paid for the third month running.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after setting the limit with Ira?
qa.a: Yash felt terrible when Ira cried but still believed the limit was right, so Yash did not change it.

qa.q: Why was sorting the lies a wise way to respond?
qa.a: It let Yash match each response to the size of the lie: letting the kind one go, mentioning the small pattern lightly, and setting a firm limit for the repeated, costly one.

qa.q: How might Ira see Yash's new rule?
qa.a: Ira might feel hurt and exposed, but the calm, clear rule also shows her exactly what she has to do to keep the flat.

grounding: Yash weighs three lies of different sizes and responds proportionately, letting a kind one go and setting a firm limit for a repeated, costly one.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Supervisor's note, QA team, 3 October. Written by Sachin.
This week Tejas, our twenty-five-year-old team lead, dealt with two lies. I watched how he weighed them.
On Monday an intern messaged "five minutes away" and arrived forty minutes later. Tejas said to her, privately and with a half-smile, "Next time just say forty. It's fine." Nothing more.
On Wednesday he found that one tester had marked the same failing test as "passed" three times in a month, and the release went out with the bug. Tejas did not smile. He met the tester with HR, laid out the three dates, and said, "This isn't one mistake. It's a pattern, and it put a bug in front of customers. You're off release sign-offs until further notice, and this goes on your record."
He told me later, "I didn't want to treat both the same."
Next step: I have asked Tejas to share his approach with the other team leads.

qa.q: How many times had the tester marked the failing test as passed?
qa.a: The tester marked it as passed three times in a month.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel about treating the two lies the same way?
qa.a: Tejas was reluctant to treat both lies the same; he cared about being fair and wanted each response to match the lie's size and cost.

qa.q: What made Tejas's responses fitting?
qa.a: He handled the intern's small social fib lightly and privately, but treated the tester's repeated, costly lie seriously with HR, clear facts and firm limits.

qa.q: How might the intern have felt after Tejas's half-smile comment?
qa.a: The intern was probably relieved and a little embarrassed, and likely to be more honest about timing without feeling humiliated.

grounding: A supervisor records a young team lead weighing a small social lie against a repeated, costly one and responding in proportion, with firm limits for the serious pattern.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Sunday
Sorting out my thoughts about Pradeep, because I've been annoyed all week and I want to be fair.
Lie one: he told Amma her rasam was "the best in Chennai". It wasn't; he left half. That's just kindness. Not touching that.
Lie two: "stuck in traffic" three times this month, when I could see from the office window he was still at the tea stall. That's a pattern, and it wastes my time. I'll tell him straight on Monday: I'd rather hear "I'm running late" than a story.
Lie three: on Thursday he told the client the delay was because I sent the drawings late. I sent them on Tuesday. I have the email. That one isn't small. It cost me with a client I've spent two years building.
For that one I'm going to our lead with the email, and I'm not sharing client work with Pradeep again until he fixes it himself.
Writing it down helps. They're not all the same lie.
Kalyani

qa.q: When did Kalyani actually send the drawings?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel about Pradeep this week?
qa.a: Kalyani felt annoyed all week but wanted to be fair, sorting the lies instead of reacting to all of them the same way.

qa.q: How did Kalyani match the response to each lie?
qa.a: Ignoring the kind rasam comment, speaking directly about the traffic excuses, and taking the client lie to the lead with the email and stopping shared client work.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Kalyani's different responses?
qa.a: Pradeep may be surprised the traffic excuses were noticed, and will learn from the firm limit that blaming Kalyani to a client crossed a real line.

grounding: Shows a colleague weighing a social white lie, a pattern of excuses and a serious betrayal, and responding in proportion to each.

Ganga: need a sanity check. is it bad I'm upset with Nisha
Gautam: what happened
Ganga: two things. yesterday she said she loved the mug I got her. it's already at the back of the cupboard 🙂
Gautam: that's just being nice
Ganga: agreed. not bothered. but the other thing
Ganga: third month she's said she paid her electricity share. landlord called today. she hasn't. we got a warning notice
Gautam: ok that's different
Ganga: yeah. one is manners. one is a pattern that costs me money and my rental record
Gautam: what are you going to do
Ganga: talk tonight, calmly. show her the notice. and from now we pay the landlord separately, I'm not covering again
Gautam: and if she lies about it again?
Ganga: then I'm looking for a new flatmate. I mean it
Gautam: sounds fair tbh

qa.q: What did the landlord's call reveal?
qa.a: Nisha hasn't paid the electricity share, and they got a warning notice.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel about the two lies?
qa.a: Ganga is not bothered by the mug lie but upset and worried about the electricity one, which costs money and a rental record.

qa.q: How is Ganga's plan proportionate?
qa.a: Letting the polite lie go, talking calmly about the repeated one with the notice, paying the landlord separately, and setting a firm limit if it happens again.

qa.q: How might Nisha feel tonight when Ganga shows her the notice?
qa.a: Nisha may feel caught and embarrassed, since the landlord's call leaves little room for another story.

grounding: Shows a young woman separating a polite white lie from a repeated lie with real cost, and setting a firm, proportionate limit.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
In the tailoring shop above the bus stand in Sinnar, Leela sat with her tea and her apprentice's week in her head.
Aditi had told old Mrs Pawar her faded blouse "looked like new". It didn't. Leela smiled at that; it was manners.
Aditi had told two customers "ready by tomorrow" and then asked for another day. That was a pattern, but a small one. Leela would teach her to say "Thursday" and mean it.
But the bride's blouse was different. Aditi had said she'd taken all the measurements herself. She hadn't; she'd guessed from an old blouse. Now it didn't close, the wedding was in four days, and the family was upset.
When Aditi came in, Leela didn't shout. "The blouse is a serious one. You'll stay late with me tonight to recut it, and you'll phone the family and tell them the truth yourself. And from now on I check every measurement you take, until I say otherwise."
Aditi nodded, eyes wet.

qa.q: What had Aditi told old Mrs Pawar?
qa.a: That her faded blouse 'looked like new'.

qa.q: How did Leela feel about each of Aditi's lies?
qa.a: Leela was amused by the polite lie, mildly concerned about the missed deadlines, and serious and firm about the bride's blouse.

qa.q: How was Leela's response proportionate?
qa.a: She let the courtesy go, planned to teach realistic deadlines, and for the serious lie set firm limits: recutting that night, Aditi phoning the family, and every measurement checked.

qa.q: What was that evening like for Aditi?
qa.a: Aditi was tearful and ashamed, facing a late night and a hard call to the bride's family, though she was not shouted at.

grounding: Shows a shop owner weighing an apprentice's polite lie, a small pattern and a costly lie, and responding in proportion with firm limits for the serious one.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
By Thursday Nadia had a small list in her head, and she sorted it on the tram home from the animal clinic in Lyon.

Monday: Aiko told Mrs Durand her knitted dog blanket was "perfect". It was lumpy. Nadia had smiled; that one cost nobody anything.

Tuesday and Wednesday: "Five minutes away!" when Aiko was clearly still at home. Annoying. Worth one honest word, not a war.

Today: the chart said the old beagle in kennel three had had his evening tablet. The tablet was still in the tray. It was the second time this month.

Nadia's stomach tightened. That wasn't smoothing anything over; an animal could suffer.

Two stops before her own, she got off and went back. She put the chart and the tray in front of Dr Morel, who gave the beagle his tablet at once. Then she found Aiko by the lockers. "I told Dr Morel about the chart. The late texts I can live with. This I can't."

qa.q: Where was the old beagle kept?
qa.a: The old beagle was in kennel three.

qa.q: What did Nadia feel when she saw the tablet still in the tray?
qa.a: Nadia felt alarmed; her stomach tightened because an animal could suffer, and it was the second time this month.

qa.q: Which of Nadia's choices matched the size of each lie?
qa.a: She let the kind blanket comment go, planned one honest word about the late texts, and took the repeated false chart to Dr Morel that same evening, setting a firm limit only where real harm was possible.

qa.q: How might Aiko experience Nadia's different reactions?
qa.a: Aiko may feel stung or defensive about the report, but the smile over the blanket and the calm plan about lateness show Nadia is not punishing every small untruth.

grounding: Shows an observer weighing someone's lies by their cost: a kind social untruth, an annoying pattern, and a repeated serious lie that gets a firm, proportionate response.
